title: 7 Strategies to Make Content Stick
author: Beaton, Erica
summary: In this guest post, high school English and history teacher Erica Beaton argues that students' forgetting of previously taught content wastes precious instructional time, and that cognitive-science research, specifically Make It Stick, shows how to fix it. She urges teachers to explain to students how learning works, including neuroplasticity, and to debunk the learning-styles myth, which she has dropped from her own planning. She argues that teachers must explicitly teach students how to study, discrediting rereading, highlighting and cramming in favor of desirable difficulties. Her recommended strategies include frequent low-stakes and cumulative quizzing, self-quizzing, spaced retrieval with flashcards, interleaving topics, and attention to sleep. Throughout, she ties each research finding to concrete practices from her own classroom and to her own struggle with perfectionism, encouraging students to embrace the struggle of effortful learning.
points: Beaton argues that reteaching forgotten content each year is a costly waste, and that research-based retention strategies are the remedy.
She has abandoned planning around learning styles, now asking what a lesson costs in precise and enduring retention.
Teachers must explicitly teach students how to study, because leaving that to children is neither fair nor efficient.
Rereading notes creates an illusion of mastery, so she replaces it with self-quizzing, spaced retrieval and cumulative quizzes.
Interleaving study across subjects forces students to find the underlying principles that connect isolated facts.
quotes: Yes, I am irked by the fifteen-year-old who doesn't remember to bring a pencil to the final exam, but I am more concerned about the junior who doesn't remember who won the Civil War, which was taught only three years prior in eighth grade, or the sophomore who can't identify the subject and verb of a simple sentence, which seems like it needs to be retaught every year in ELA.

It has direct correlation on their ability to learn. Even though, I don't teach psychology, I explicitly teach my English and US History classes about the brain. I show them this video on neuroplasticity. We read Articles of the Week about learning and the brain. We talk about it until they understand how learning works. When that happens, their learning becomes more efficacious.

Moreover, if I'm planning a new lesson, I used to ask: “How can I meet my kinesthetic, musical, and visual learners? Now, I ask: “What cost would I pay to ‘precise and enduring' content retention if I spend time addressing these various preferences?
Even if we figured out how to study on our own, it isn't fair or cost-effective to leave this “figuring out” to a bunch of children. We'd be wasting our time by not “slowing down to run fast.

I use cumulative quizzes with our study of vocabulary and literacy devices in English. In US History, I'm more purposeful about designing quizzes that reach back to concepts covered in earlier units to recirculate our learning. I also give a lot of practice quizzes where “the points don't matter.

If we keep going over the same content, it will feel like we've learned the content, but really this immediate recollection creates a false security of knowing. We need to embrace the difficulty of spaced retrieval.

I want to be transparent about the frustrations and difficulties of learning—not just sympathizing with their trials but continuing to practice vulnerability with them. In the last two years, I've shared with my students a little about how my perfectionism gets in the way of the things I want to do and the stress this causes because recognizing where we have learning gaps is half the battle.
